name: Treaty with the Seneca and Shawnee, 1832
aka: Treaty with the United Nation of Senecas and Shawnees
nations: Seneca of Sandusky and the mixed band of Seneca and Shawnee of Lewistown, Ohio, who formed the United Nation of Senecas and Shawnees
promises: Article 1: the United Nation of Senecas and Shawnees gave up the land granted to them west of the Neosho (Grand) River by the treaties of 1831.

Article 2: the United States would grant them by letters patent, in fee simple, a tract east of the Neosho between the Missouri line and the Cherokee line, 60,000 acres plus the Sandusky Seneca land, not to be sold without the consent of the United States.
Article 3: the United States would build a grist mill, saw mill and blacksmith shop.
Article 4: the United States would pay $1,000 for removal losses.
landTaken: Royce Areas 498 to 504, attached to this id, are cessions from these lands under the treaty of February 23, 1867, assigned to the Wyandot, the Peoria and confederated tribes, and the Ottawa (Royce schedule).
today: No court, Claims Commission or government finding on this treaty or on the 1867 cession of its lands was located. The Commission transferred Seneca-Cayuga Dockets 341-A to D to the Court of Claims on September 29, 1978, when only attorney expense applications were pending in them.

openQuestions: The Royce areas on this id were ceded in 1867, not 1832; the queue's scheduleTribes list the tribes later assigned the land, not the parties to this treaty.
What Dockets 341-A to D claimed and how they were decided was not traced.
No Seneca-Cayuga Nation or Eastern Shawnee Tribe account of this treaty was found.
Which present-day nations succeed the Lewistown band (the queue lists Seneca-Cayuga and Shawnee tribes) was not confirmed from a nation's own source.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for seneca, shawnee, Lewistown, December 29 1832 and 7 Stat. 411; Dockets 341-A and 341-B (1971-1974) concern the 1831 Sandusky and Lewistown treaties and the 1867 merger of funds, and only mention this treaty as the confederation; no Court of Claims case names it. Nothing new.

nationVoice.summary: The history the Nation publishes on its website (Muriel H. Wright's text from A Guide to the Indian Tribes of Oklahoma) says the Seneca of Sandusky reached the Cowskin River in 1832 after an eight-month removal from Ohio marked by delay and great suffering, and that the treaty made at the Seneca Agency on December 29, 1832 joined them with the Mixed Band of Seneca and Shawnee as the United Nation of Seneca and Shawnees, dividing the tract east of the Neosho between the two groups.

A 2020 post on the Nation's website says the Cayuga among its founders came from the Sandusky, Ohio area and the Seneca from New York and Canada, that both were moved to Oklahoma under Indian removal, and that, too few to stand alone, they joined as one nation and adopted a constitution in 1937.
